entries.title: Plan writer cost: sub-planners per part, and twill versus a solo writer
entries.brief: The Plan writer is 18% of spend; sub-planners per part for large bundles, and a twill versus solo Opus high comparison on cost, rounds and time
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/tokens/token-audit-2026-10-22`: the Plan writer is the costliest session type, about $8 per run, $1,306 with its forks over two weeks (18% of all spend).
It averages 81 turns at a mean context of 223k, holds 153k by its first fork and peaks around 308k, mostly from about 71 raw `sed -n`/`grep` code reads.
Every `twill-plan` lens fork inherits that context, about 287k per turn; since 2026-10-20 the writer and its forks cost about $18 per run.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Fork the lenses earlier, before the code reads pile up, or hand the writer a digest of the code it needs instead of raw reads.
Cutting a quarter of the writer's and its forks' cost saves about 4.5% of all spend; quality must be benched first.

## Discussion with the operator (2026-10-22)

- A code digest instead of raw reads is rejected: it is too inexact unless the code itself is read, and the writer would read the source anyway to be sure.
  Finding what to read is already `relevant.md`'s job; whether the writer uses it is worth measuring (how much of what the writer read the list named).
- Lens forks as fresh agents are rejected: that is the perch itself.
- Sub-planners: Discussion splits the scope into parts in the decision record, groups `relevant.md` per part, and each sub-planner reads only its part; the lead owns the shared spots and joins the card DAG.
  This keeps every review round and matters more as loom tasks are bundled larger.
  Review could split per part the same way, since each fresh reviewer rebuilds its context every round (Plan reviewer: 48 turns at 123k mean context, $2.48 per session).
- Twill-plan versus a solo writer: since the full `twill-plan` fan (2026-10-20), 7 landed loom runs average 2.00 Plan rounds against 2.09 before, while the writer's forks cost about $7 per run and a Plan round about $3.70; too few runs to judge.
  The operator sees strong signs that the twill writer makes a far better one-shot plan in shorter time, and time counts as well as tokens.
  Still, test a solo Opus high writer: compare twill, solo Opus high and solo Fable on Plan cost, Plan rounds and Plan wall time (`lym report timing`) per run.

## Split writing: two variants to bench (operator, 2026-10-22)

Discussion-Write and Plan-Write already run as `shedadapters.MultiLLMProducer` over a `seatengine` table, a chair and advisors; advisors only advise, and twill is the chair forking itself, so today one session writes the whole product.
Two ways to have parts written separately, both benched against each other and against the twill and solo writers before anything reaches production:

1. **Seats with writing assistants.** The chair splits the scope, fixes the interfaces and shared spots, and hands each assistant seat its part; it then joins and checks the parts.
   A new seat role beside the advisor.
   Risks: assistants see neither each other's work nor a shared context, so seams fall to the chair and review, and overlapping parts make several seats read the same code.
2. **Fork-based.** The chair keeps its context lean (scope, split and shared spots only) and forks once per part, so every part writer inherits the same overview without the writer's full reading.
   Technically still one writer with forks, like twill but forking early.

## Data check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Plan writer plus its lens forks, means per run (API list price):

| group | runs | writer+forks | forks | Plan-Write wall | Plan rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before 10-15 (solo writer) | 28 | $9.08 | $0.58 | 16.4 min active | 1.3 |
| 10-15 to 10-19 | 41 | $9.39 | $3.86 | 18.5 min | 1.88 |
| 10-20 to c62274be5 (full twill-plan fan) | 7 | $18.14 | $7.66 | 23.9 min | 2.00 |
| after c62274be5 (five lenses) | 3 | $16.64 | $7.40 | 23.9 min | 1.33 |

- The later groups are larger tasks, so the cost rise is not the fan alone; the five-lens group is too small to judge.
- `relevant.md` use, over 32 runs with a list and a Plan-Write transcript: 85% of named files were read, but only 28% of read files were named (about 3.5 files read per file named, about 7 on large runs). Both shares are lower bounds (directory greps and quarry reads not counted).
- So `relevant.md` works as a floor, not a boundary; most unnamed reading looks like tests and neighbouring callers, which a per-part split of the list would not remove.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench; the split-writing variant has since been built and benched against `Plan-Write` (see the last section).
- Scripts, baseline tables and `results.md` are in `docs/research/loom/plan-writer-audit-2026-10-24/`; rerun per its README.

## Discussion versus Plan: double reading (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-25)

55 loom runs seeded 2026-10-15 or later with both a `ly:<slug>:discussion` and a `ly:<slug>:plan` transcript on this machine; cost at API list price from the 10-24 tokencount reports, per run:

| | Discussion | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| phase total (writer, forks, review, fix) | $8.68 | $18.51 |
| writer session alone | $2.07 | $6.60 |
| writer turns / mean context | 39 / 89k tokens | 83 / 183k tokens |
| repo files read by the writer (pooled) | 1,093 | 3,286 |
| share read by both | 62% of Discussion's reads re-read by Plan | 21% of Plan's reads read by Discussion |
| same, without `PATTERN.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `pattern/`, `docs/` | 64% | 20% |

- Discussion costs 0.47 of Plan for the phase and 0.31 for the writer alone; Discussion was the dearer phase in only 4 of 55 runs.
- Plan-Write re-reads about 62% of the files Discussion-Write read (mean of per-run shares 62%), so exploration is repeated, but Plan reads about three times as many files and most of its reading (79%) is new.
- Rough size of the repeat: the Plan-Write reads that Discussion had already made are about 3.3M tokens pooled, about 59k per run (file bytes at current `main` divided by 4; whole files assumed, so an upper bound).
  That is roughly a third of the Plan writer's mean context, and it is paid again on every later turn through the cache.
- File-level only: directory greps, globs and `lym quarry` reads are not counted, and a file is the same file by path, not by the lines read.
- The Discussion phase total holds its review rounds and fixers, which is most of its cost beyond the writer; the segment figures come from the 10-24 tokencount reports, so runs landed since are priced as of then.
- Rerun: `.scratch/discussion-overlap/reads2.sh <slug> plan|discussion` per run, then `analyze.sh`; both stay in `.scratch` and are not committed.
- Decision (operator, 2026-10-25): Discussion stays a separate step; folding it into the Plan writer would add turns to the costliest session.

## Turn audit (landed 2026-10-28)

`docs/research/turns/turn-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` (n = 1 loom run, 213 sessions) finds the Plan writer spends 33 of its 101 turns on serial single-call reads and searches, mostly shell `grep` and `sed -n`, which a merged turn would remove.
It recommends one stencil sentence in `loom-template-plan.md` and in the twill lens directive: issue every search and read you can name in one message.
This is a cheaper cut than the digest, the earlier fork and the split writing above, and the audit proposes no pre-read for the writer.
The Plan row rests on one session; the recommendation was later applied and measured, see the next section.

## Batching effect audit (landed 2026-11-01)

The turn audit's recommendation above was applied (the batching sentences of `bf00a043`, 2026-10-28), and `docs/research/turns/batching-effect-audit-2026-11-01/report.md` measured it on 8 runs, 7 landed (5 before, 2 after).
It finds no batching effect, and the sample cannot show a small one: the Plan writer issued 1.14 calls per turn after against 1.29 before, its single-call turn share was 83% against 75%, and its serial read and search turns were 44% of its turns against 41%.
The Discussion writer is level on every measure.
The 33-of-101 serial turns the turn audit found are still there, so the ideas above keep their value.

## Batching moved to heddle (landed 2026-11-01)

`plan-edits-before-gate` (`1834cebf`) removed the batching sentences from the stencils, `loom-template-plan.md`, `loom-template-discussion.md` and `twill-directive.md` among them.
The one rule (read in one message, decide every edit, make them in one message, one gate run) is now the shipped heddle entry `lym-plan-edits-before-gate`, rendered after `lym-batching`.
Its effect on agent behaviour is not measured; `agent-turns-effect` measures it.
Task `turn-savings-measure` (`3207d97e`, 2026-11-04) has since measured project `agent-turns` as a whole in `docs/research/turns/turn-savings-measure-2026-11-04/report.md`, over the 20 most recent darn runs and 4 tapestry runs: the darn writer issues 2.05 calls a turn against 1.08, and shell edits fall from 339 calls to 21.
The report covers darn and Webster, not the Plan writer's serial lookups, so those stay unmeasured here.
Task `batching-hook-remeasure` (`d05c8d75`, 2026-11-05, `docs/research/turns/batching-hook-remeasure-2026-11-05/report.md`) has since measured the rule's effect on edit chains: edit follows rose from 4.2% to 6.9% of context, all mid-round and none after a failed gate, so the rule does not stop mid-round edit splitting; its one open question is the hook's live gap, note `batching-hook-live-gap`.
`plan-reviewer-batching` (`5227aeaa`) added a wave structure for the fanned Plan reviewer's pre-read in `burler-fork-reading.md`; it too is unmeasured.

## Writer lookups measured (landed 2026-11-04)

Task `planner-fork-lookups` (`482c05d4`, `docs/research/turns/writer-lookups-measure-2026-11-04/report.md`) measured the Plan and Discussion writers' exploration on 7 sessions of 3 tapestry runs, with no agent run.
- The 3 Plan writers each handed one batch of 3 or 4 `sonnet` lookup subagents to the Agent tool in one message; 1 of 3 full Discussion sessions did.
- Exploration is 46% of the writers' cost ($11.03 of $23.76); 15% of it is paid above 200k context, every chain above 200k is in a Plan session after its one batch, and 3 of the 6 are single-call serial lookups.
- Moving every search turn to subagents would save at most about $4.7, one fifth of writer spend; for the short late chains, batching in the writer saves more.
- The report recommends no bench of the excerpt cut below and no stronger stencil now, and a re-run once more tapestry runs have landed.
Task `batching-hook-reach` (`119c1c05`, 2026-11-04) made the batching nudge hook count read-only Bash lookups and reach subagents and forks, so the writer's serial `grep` and `sed -n` chains are what it nudges.
Task `batching-hook-remeasure` (`d05c8d75`, 2026-11-05) measured it on 22 runs: the hook fired 13 times, about 2.5% of the breach turns it was built for, the breach shares did not fall where it reaches, and the report recommends removing it; the live gap is note `batching-hook-live-gap`.

## Split writing built and benched (landed 2026-11-01)

The second variant above exists as two opt-in producers: `Parts-Write` splits the task into parts with contracts and shared spots, and `Parts-Plan-Write` runs one fresh writer session per part under a joining chair.
Both sit behind the tapestry flag `plan_split` (off by default; `Plan-Write` stays the default), and the joined plan passes the ordinary `plan` gate.

`plan-split-bench` (`989a8b85`, `docs/research/loom/plan-split/plan-split-bench-2026-11-01/`) benched them against `Plan-Write` on replays of `warp-visibility` and `run-verbs-shared`, one Plan-Review round each.
- `warp-visibility`: the split cost $16.69 against $14.93 and took 15m39s against 25m07s; its largest session peaked at 245k context against 408k.
  The split plan had 34 cards against 15 and its review found 4 blocking findings against 3.
- `run-verbs-shared`: the plan arm cost $28.03 with a 674k peak; the split arm failed when reed lost the chair strand (note `reed-loses-parts-chair`), so there is no comparison.
- The joined split plan passed its gate only after two hand edits to `parts.md`, both defects of `Parts-Write`; the report recommends keeping `plan_split` off.

## Split writers tuned, round 1 (landed 2026-11-02)

Task `plan-split-tune` (`fe753d40`, `docs/research/loom/plan-split/plan-split-tune-2026-11-02/report.md`) landed round 1 with no replay.
The parts gate and `lym loom validate-parts` now refuse an export that is an existing member or path (`export-existing`) and run the name checks on each `plan:` export, and `Parts-Write` reads the PATTERN entries governing each export's name first.

## Split writers replayed (landed 2026-11-03)

Task `plan-split-replay` (`e9b4c949`, same report, which now covers both tasks) replayed both inputs on the installed `lym`, built after the tuning landed.
- Both inputs joined their parts into a plan in round 1 and passed their gates with no hand edit of `parts.md` or the part plans, so the loop ended after round 1 of its cap of 2 and no further tuning was made.
- `warp-visibility`: $18.69 writing cost, 36 cards, one `plan-part` refusal cleared on the gate's re-prompt. `run-verbs-shared`: $29.36, 37 cards, no refusal.
- Plan-Review found no blocking finding on either plan (8 and 12 findings); the fixer was not run, so those findings stand unresolved.
- One run per input is a direction, not an effect.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench.

## Data point: `cold-gate-fixer` Plan-Write (orch, 2026-11-02)

One loom run, read from the writer's transcript and its subagents' by a read-only agent; the numbers are the writer's own context, by last turn usage.

- The writer made 45 tool calls in about 25 turns before it started `fork0`: 22 Reads (18 whole-file, 4 slices), 16 Bash calls (about 14 single lookups, 2 `cat` of whole files), 5 Agent calls and 2 skill loads.
- The writer followed the Sonnet-subagent rule: five read-only `general-purpose` agents with `model: sonnet`, launched together at 115k context.
  Each ended at 39k to 73k and ran 33 to 61 seconds; their answers added little to the writer.
  The 115k they were started at had already come from the writer's own whole-file Reads and `cat`s, so the subagents did not keep the reading out of the writer's context.
- `fork0` (Opus) started at 198k, inherited it, ran 17 minutes and ended at 338k; the writer was at 204k when it returned.
- After `fork0` returned, the writer read all 14 plan files back in one batch, 35k tokens (205k to 240k), the largest jump of the later phase.
  The five lens forks then started at 243k and added 2k to 20k each; the lens fixes, 8 more files and 24 edits in a row took the writer to 332k.
- The phase took about 31 minutes: exploration about 3, `fork0` 17, lens review about 3, and about 5 idle waiting on `validate-plan` and the lens forks.
- No compaction and no threshold event fired.

Reading: the writer must read much to write a joined plan, and `fork0` gets that reading for free by inheriting it, so the cost is the 198k each fork carries, not the reading itself.
Two cuts remain open: have the first exploration fan answer with the lines needed (sonnet reads, writer gets excerpts) instead of the writer reading whole files after it, and skip the read-back of every plan file when `fork0` has already validated them.

### Correction (operator, 2026-11-02)

The second cut above, skipping the read-back of the plan files after `fork0`, is rejected.
The read-back is needed: the writer gets the plan from `fork0` without `fork0`'s reasoning, so it must read the plan to judge it, and the lens forks then review a plan whose reasoning nobody carries, which makes them the more critical check.
Only the first cut (excerpts from the exploration fan instead of whole-file Reads by the writer) stays open.

entries.title: A closed area for lym: bwrap sandbox in stages, off by default
entries.brief: Run the lym process tree in a bwrap area with a host proxy and broker, built in three stages with a stop; to be split if it goes ahead
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-30)

Every agent lym starts runs with `--dangerously-skip-permissions`, which many people do not accept, and a repository that states it supports safe sandboxing is worth more than one that does not.
The operator uses lym alone, on Linux (OSL-1046: Ubuntu 24.04; Neve: Kubuntu on Ubuntu 26.04, Plasma 6), and has no interest in other users or in Windows.
The research is `docs/research/platform/sandboxing-options-2026-10-30.md`: it weighs `bwrap`, Landlock, a dedicated Linux user, systemd sandboxing, podman and Claude Code's own `/sandbox`, and the packages and cards each would change.

Two exposures hold today with no area: an agent can reach `/run/user/<uid>/bus` and through it `systemd-run --user`, which starts any process outside lym's tree, and it can type into other hubs' tmux panes through their sockets in `/tmp/tmux-<uid>`, the Models hub's among them.

## Idea

Run the whole lym process tree inside a `bwrap` area launched by lym itself, with the agents free inside it and a short, controlled list of exits.
It is an option the operator turns on, never a requirement: with it off, everything works as it does today, and with it on, nothing starts when the sandbox cannot.
The operator thinks the full design is complicated and error-prone, and doubts it will work without large problems, so it is built in stages with a stop between them.
This is one large note and is split into tasks, or a project, only when the operator decides it goes ahead.

### Before the area: two cheap steps

- Start a hub's tmux server from a Konsole window, not a VS Code terminal: the server inherits the `vscode` AppArmor profile, which grants user namespaces to every agent of the hub.
- A line in `README.md` that every agent lym starts runs with bypass permissions, and that lym belongs on a machine the operator is willing to hand to its agents.

### Stage 1: the filesystem area only

`bwrap` with `--unshare-all --die-with-parent --clearenv` around reed's tmux server and everything under it, started by a new `lym area start` and a supervisor inside.

- The hub is bound read-write at its own path, since the tmux server name, the creel socket name, git's worktree links and Claude Code's transcript directory all derive from absolute paths; `/usr`, `/etc` and `/opt` are read-only, `$HOME` a tmpfs with read-only binds of the Go toolchain, the Claude Code binary and the installed `lym`.
- The area has its own Claude config directory and Go caches bound at the usual paths, with the host's plugin cache read-only on top, so the host's `settings.json` hooks never run in it.
- One host directory holds the tmux socket directory, so `lym reed attach` from outside drives the server inside; tried on OSL-1046 with a tmux server inside `bwrap`.
- `.git/hooks` is read-only; `.git/config` was to stay writable for `branch.<b>.lymLocal`, but `fabric-remote-async` removed that mark and `internal/gitrepo/branchmark.go`, so the reason is gone; whether git itself or another lym writer still needs `.git/config` writable is unchecked.
- Network stays open and there is no broker, so the landing deploy, `lym reed window`, `lym ide` and `lym hibernate request` do not work from inside; the operator does them by hand, from outside.
- A config module `area` with `required`, off by default; `lym area start` refuses on any failure and never falls back to an unsandboxed start.
- Ubuntu 24.04 needs a one-time AppArmor profile for `/usr/bin/bwrap`, loaded by root; the report names the profile, and Ubuntu 25.04 and later ship it, which is not verified on Neve.

This closes the two exposures above and shows early whether tmux, creel and dobby run well inside an area.

### Stop: the operator decides whether stage 1 works well enough to go on.

### Stage 2: egress through a host proxy

No network inside the area; a host-side proxy, reached through a bound socket, allows CONNECT to `api.anthropic.com`, `claude.ai`, `platform.claude.com`, `proxy.golang.org`, `sum.golang.org`, `github.com` and `api.github.com`, with a loopback relay inside the area.
Telemetry and the auto-updater are off by environment.
The GitHub token handed to the area is fine-grained and limited to the hub's repositories; the operator's `gh` login never enters.
WebFetch and the `prowler` skill reach only these hosts.

### Stage 3: a broker for the remaining exits

A host-side process serving a fixed set of verbs and never a command line from the area: the landing deploy (it fetches `origin/main` into its own clone, checks the commit is the tip, builds with the host's Go and installs), `lym reed window` opening Konsole, and `lym hibernate request`.
`lym ide` is refused, since VS Code on the host would run git over repositories the area writes; the host runs no git over the area's repositories at all.

## What is not claimed

Isolation from a kernel exploit, which needs a virtual machine; that data in the area cannot leave through an allowed host; and that a landed change of lym itself cannot run on the host once deployed, which matters on this hub because it develops lym.
Landlock stays a possible inner layer once both machines run a kernel with ABI 9 and 10, and Claude Code deny rules in shuttle's settings are a cheap second line inside the area; the dedicated user, podman, systemd sandboxing and Claude Code's `/sandbox` inside lym runs are left out.
The report estimates the whole at five tasks and eighteen cards.

## Related

Note `creel-cross-hub-mail`: the inbox folder sits outside an area, so reading and writing it goes through the broker.

entries.title: An interactive agent idle for a set time gets its session compacted
entries.brief: lym asks an idle interactive agent to commit what it has and end, and the run resumes later
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-31)

An interactive run (the `sampler` recipe, landed by task `interactive-recipe`) waits for the operator in its pane at the `Sampler-Session` row, and has dobby's quiet notice and the step watchdog off while it does.
The row waits with no timeout until the agent runs `lym loom sampler-done` at the operator's word.
Since lym runs the agent, it can watch how long the agent has waited.

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-03)

An auto-compact mode, in place of the earlier idea of parking the run:

- When an interactive agent has been idle for a set time, lym compacts its session, the way `lym orch distill` compacts the orch, and the agent stays in its pane with the run still at its row.
- The operator comes back to the same session with a small context, so nothing is ended, committed or resumed by hand.
- The idle time is a config key; off means never.

The earlier idea, writing down the state, committing it, ending the session and pausing the run, is dropped: it is too specific to be worth its cost.

entries.title: The decision record on the board, and splitting a discussed task
entries.brief: A task flagged discussed carries its decision record on the board and skips Discussion; three ways to split, from by hand to stitch
entries.body:
## Seen

A task's decision record lived only in its run's weft (`_lym/discussion/decision-record.md`): a cancelled run left it in the records history, and no new task took it along.
So when Discussion finds a task too large, or the operator decides a tapestry run should rather be split, what Discussion found is lost or must be copied out by hand.
Several notes circled the same question (where the decision record lives, how a task is split); this note joins them.

## Names (operator, 2026-11-03)

A board idea is a note; the decision record that Discussion, or the recipe `motif`, makes is a Sketch, written with a capital S as a proper name, so it does not read as a loose draft; a finished plan may later be a cartoon.
Code still says "decision record": nothing in code is renamed to Sketch, except the board type below.
Since 2026-11-05 an entry that holds a motif run's record is also a Sketch on the board: a note of the built-in type `sketch`.

## Core: the decision record on the board (operator, 2026-11-01)

- When Discussion is approved, after its review, the decision record is copied into the task's board entry, and the entry is flagged as discussed.
- A task flagged discussed skips Discussion: tapestry starts at Plan from the record, and darn takes the record as final, as darn takes its task text as already discussed today.
- Changing one's mind loses nothing: the run is cancelled, the record stays on the board, and it can be split into discussed tasks or made a project.
- lym itself writes the record field, at Discussion's approval and at each `lym loom decision add`, so the field is exempt from the lock on a claimed entry.
  That lock exists only so the orch does not change a task's text after its agents have read it; a record written by lym is not that.
- Built (2026-11-03): task `decision-record-on-board` stores the record and the flag.
  The record is the file `decision-<slug>.md` at the Bolt root beside `board.json`, which carries only a `discussed` boolean; `lym board get` shows the flag and `--record` prints the record; `lym loom decision store` re-copies it by hand.
  Runs already past Discussion are not backfilled.
- Built (2026-11-03): task `readme-shows-discussed` (`1bbcc3b1`).
  The board README and every project file link a discussed entry's record as `Sketch` under its slug, Done entries included.
- Built (2026-11-07, `c5e44a93`): the design page of every discussed entry also carries a `Decision record: [Sketch](decision-<slug>.md)` line under its metadata line, so a reader who opens the page from the board reaches the record.
  `RenderToDisk` renders a discussed entry whose record file is missing as undiscussed, so no page links a missing record.
- Built (2026-11-03): task `shed-sub-run-block` adds the block row and the recipe `motif` (tapestry's Discussion rows).
- Built (2026-11-03): task `tapestry-motif-block`.
  Tapestry defines Discussion once, in `motif-recipe.yaml`, and runs it through a block row named `Motif`.
  The block's gate `undiscussed` passes the block over when the entry is flagged discussed: the stored record is seeded as the run's decision record and the run goes on at Drift-Baseline, so Plan-Write and the reviews read it as they read an approved one.
  Approval inside the block stores the record.
  The trial recipe `arras` is removed.
- Built (2026-11-05): task `raddle-recipe` (`257ab79a`).
  Record-Write copies a discussed entry's stored record into the run's decision record for every recipe with that row, so a darn entry flagged `discussed` now builds from its stored record.
  That closes the former open point that darn take the stored record as final.

## Discussion as a run of its own (operator, 2026-11-03)

How a task is best cut into smaller tasks is known only once its Discussion is done, so the split comes after Discussion, not before.

- A Discussion-only run, the recipe `motif` (operator, 2026-11-03: the motif is the design decided before the weaving; `cartoon`, the drawing the weaver follows, is kept for a later Plan block), interactive or not, runs Discussion-Write and its review and nothing else, then stores the record and flags the entry discussed, as the core above says.
  Built (2026-11-03): a `motif` task runs alone and lands no code; landing only prunes the board.
  Built (2026-11-05): task `sketch-board-type` (`f2ae537d`).
  A finished motif run no longer leaves the task `discussed`: the entry becomes a Sketch, a note of the built-in type `sketch` (handle letter `S`) that keeps its module labels and loses its status and the fields only a run, a landing or the dependency graph read (`depends_on`, `isolated`, `recipe`, `profile`, `run_settings`, `pull_request`, `notify_on_land`).
  A Sketch is not a task and never runs.
  The board lists Sketches last in `lym board list --text` and first among the Notes in the README; the `Discussed` README layer is gone, and every board write turns an older open `discussed` task into a Sketch.
  A Sketch another entry depends on is refused: the entry stays `draft` with a warning.
  Built (2026-11-03): task `beam-after-motif` (`cfccb80a`).
  When the entry is then made a project, `lym beam create` removes the slug's done motif run, once its pair is gone, instead of refusing with `already completed`; the envelope reports it as `motif_run_cleared`.
  Seed-Child records the child recipe in batten's run directory, so a done run still tells it ran `motif`; a done motif run seeded before that has no record and still needs `lym batten cleanup --apply`.
- A discussed entry then goes one of two ways, chosen after its Discussion:
  1. Tapestry from Plan, skipping Discussion-Write: Plan-Write and Webster as today. Built, see above.
  2. The part split: the record's scope is cut into darn tasks with contracts and `depends_on`, which run independently, each a task of its own.

## Triage of a Sketch (operator, 2026-11-05)

Built (2026-11-05): task `raddle-recipe` (`257ab79a`), the recipe `raddle` (the raddle spreads the warp into sections before it is beamed).
It is a record-only loom recipe with the rows Record-Write, Raddle-Write and Raddle-File, run through batten like `motif`: a worktree of its own, a pane, a board status and notices, no code landed.
Built (2026-11-05): task `sketch-promote-raddle` (`867b4eeb`).
`lym board promote <slug>` of a Sketch, or `lym board promote S3` by handle, starts it with recipe `raddle`; `--recipe raddle` is still accepted, and any other recipe on a Sketch is refused, naming the plain promote.
A Sketch with no stored record is refused, naming `motif`.

- Raddle-Write is a cold Opus agent (loom key `raddle`, default `opus[high]`) that reads the Sketch, the board and a bounded read of code, and writes a proposal: one tapestry from Plan (way 1 above), several darn tasks (way 2), a mix, a project, or a beam, with the order as `depends_on`.
  It designs nothing; the Sketch has done that.
- Interactive by default: the operator approves the proposal in the agent's pane (`lym loom raddle-approve`), may question it and have it revise first.
  The loom key `raddle_auto_approve` files with no operator input; it stays off until the splits are tuned well enough.
- Raddle-File re-checks the board, then files every entry in one write, each with its part of the record stored and `discussed` set, creates the beam for shape `beam` and hands the Sketch slug and proposal to the beam's orch in Beam-Up.
  Built (2026-11-07, `731004c3`): filing releases nothing.
  Every filed task, project members included, stays `draft` until the operator releases it with `lym board set-status`; the earlier release step is removed.
  The proposal carries an optional `order_departures` list (`{parts, record_order, cost}`) naming each place its chain order departs from an order the Sketch states, and the interactive approval table shows a dependencies column, the departures and the draft notice.
  The stencil orders parts that share a package by the Sketch's own order first.
  The table, the departures and the draft notice are instructions to the agent, not enforced in code.
  A moved board, an invalid proposal or an approval-hash mismatch returns to Raddle-Write; the third return halts the run.
- The stencil carries the rule that a tapestry's fixed start cost often favours fewer, larger parts.
  The cost figures come from the hub's own runs: every agent session is recorded as `_lym/usage/<session>.json`, `lym report cost` gives the fixed-plus-per-size fit per recipe and profile, and `lym report raddle` compares each proposal's predicted cost with its landed parts, so the prompt can be tuned.
  A Codex session's dollar cost stays unknown, so its runs enter the report in hours alone.
- A raddle store beside `board.json` keeps each Sketch's proposals, record and filed slugs; `lym board raddle <slug>` prints a stored proposal.
- Not run end to end against a live hub yet: an interactive raddle run through approval and filing, and a `beam` shape run through Beam-Up's hand-off.

Still open here: the cold split agent below is now Raddle-Write, so its tuning follows from `lym report raddle` once runs have landed.

## The split is a cold agent of its own (operator, 2026-11-03)

Built as Raddle-Write above; what follows is the original design.

- The Sketch stays as it is: Discussion-Write writes no split and judges no seams, so a task going way 1 pays nothing for the split.
- A separate cold agent splits a discussed entry when way 2 is chosen: it reads the stored Sketch and the code the Sketch names, and proposes the parts.
- The proposal holds, per part: the Sketch decisions it builds, the packages it changes, its contract (what it takes in, delivers and exports), its `depends_on`, the Open risks and Acceptance criteria it carries, and a recipe and profile.
  It checks that no two parallel parts change the same package.
- The agent is a role of its own so it can be tuned hard: its prompt, model and effort are set apart from Discussion-Write's.
- Its proposal goes to the operator, who approves it before the entry becomes a project and its parts become tasks.
- Seen (2026-11-03): the first split, F18 `codex-engine` into project P2, was done by the orch from the Sketch's headings in a few calls, without checking packages, contracts or criteria per part; that shallow split is what this agent replaces.

## Ways to split, simplest first

1. The operator, or the board agent the prime's `board` button opens (task `board-agent-button`, `2def9684`, landed 2026-11-04; it loads `ly:board-policy` and `ly:board`), splits a discussed entry into tasks with `depends_on`, each with its part of the record and flagged discussed.
   The same agent can split an undiscussed entry before it runs, but then each part runs its own Discussion and rereads much of the same code; a tapestry part carries about $23 of fixed cost, so this pays best when the parts are darn-sized.
2. `stitch`: a stand-alone loom recipe for a large task's whole course, chosen before the run starts.
   Preflight, Discussion, a Pre-Plan producer that splits the decided scope into parts with contracts (what each takes in, delivers and exports, and which parts it depends on), a row with no agent that turns the entry into a project and files each part as a darn task, then an inner pawl run through `battenshed.NewInnerRun` that brings up the beam, waits until every part has landed and lands the beam.
   Parts run with review off; one review covers the whole diff after the last lands.
   It is tried first as a hand-run test project with the projects and beams that exist, measured against tapestry runs of the same size (`docs/research/tokens/token-audit-2026-10-22`), and built only if it saves tokens.
   The risk: tapestry's build is cheap because Webster runs on Sonnet following an Opus plan, while parts under a coarse pre-plan likely need Opus writers.

## Open

- A split record's format: each part must still pass the discussion check.
- Whether the old run's commits, if any, are kept when a run is cancelled for a split.
- `stitch`: contract precision, how large the whole-task review's fixes may be, and how often the choice between `stitch` and tapestry before the run is right.
- Settled (2026-11-03): the records live in a file of their own beside `board.json`, not in it.

entries.title: Two Claude accounts, each worktree on one of them by a configured weight
entries.brief: A claude config lists accounts with a config directory, a weight and their limit windows; a worktree picks one at its first session by weight and current headroom
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-11-02)

Spread Claude usage over two accounts, so one account's limits are not the bottleneck: each worktree uses one of the accounts, chosen by a weight.
The weights are config, for example account A twice for each use of account B, so account A carries twice the load of B on average.

## Accounts of different plans (operator, 2026-11-03)

The accounts need not be of one plan: for example a Claude Ultra account beside a Max account with about half its usage.
The plans' limit windows differ too: the operator reports that Max has a five-hour window that Ultra lacks.
So a fixed weight alone is not enough: a Max account can hit its five-hour window while its weekly share is far from spent.

- The weight sets the long-run share, from each account's plan.
- The pick also reads each account's current headroom in every window it has, and passes over an account that is near or at a limit; an account with no five-hour window is never judged by one.
- Lym today learns of a limit only when a pane shows the usage-limit message (`internal/shuttleengine/claudeengine/usagelimit.go`); reading an account's headroom before a pick is new, and the source is open: Claude Code's status line input, `/usage`, or lym's own transcript totals per config directory against a configured budget. Check what Claude Code exposes before choosing.
- This was weighed against offloading to Codex (`codex-engine`): the two-account route keeps every agent on Claude's review quality and is far smaller to build, so it is the first route to quota relief (orch, 2026-11-03).

## Seen (orch, 2026-11-02)

Lym cannot pick an account per worktree today.
`lym config claude` has no key for an account or a config directory, and a search of `internal/` found no use of `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`, so every session runs under whichever account the machine is logged in to.

Claude Code is believed to keep an account's login in a config directory that the `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` environment variable selects.
That is not verified: check it against the Claude Code documentation before anything is built.

## Built since

`lym config env` (`0d155d1a`, landed 2026-11-03) holds per-machine environment variables that lym exports to every process it starts for the hub: gate tiers, Drift steps and agent session panes.
A pane receives them through the `PaneEnv` closure on reed's geometry, exported ahead of the strand's launch command and read afresh at each launch.
It refuses `PATH` and any `LYM_` name, and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is allowed.

So a machine-wide `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` can be set today, which moves every session to one other account.
It is one value for the whole hub: the per-worktree pick, the weights and the headroom check below are still unbuilt.

Heddle's `claude-settings` target (`72390eb3`) is no source for the account: its entries live in the Bolt, which is pushed to GitHub, and account details never go into a file pushed to GitHub (operator, 2026-11-07); it also renders one file for every worktree, and the account must be chosen before Claude starts, through its environment.
The accounts and the pick stay machine-local.

## Design questions for a Discussion

- Config: a list of accounts, each with a name, a config directory, a weight and its limit windows, in the claude config; a machine-layer key, since the accounts belong to the machine.
- Choice: per worktree, never per session, so all of a run's sessions (writer, reviewers, fixers, driver) share one account.
  The pick is made once, when the worktree's first session starts, and recorded with the worktree so a resume, a re-attach and a hand pass keep it.
  With headroom in the pick, a deterministic hash of the slug no longer suffices: a persisted weighted counter that skips an account short of headroom is the candidate.
- Scope: the prime's orch and each beam's orch and dobby need a rule of their own, since they outlive a task run.
- A session spawn sets the chosen account's environment in one place in the claude engine's launch, so no caller sets it.
  The pane launch now already exports the `env` module's variables ahead of the launch command (`reedengine/panebin.go`); the account's variable would sit beside them, and its precedence over the module's is to be decided.
- A usage limit on one account: whether lym moves a worktree to the other account when one is limited, or only reports it; the first needs the session's history to be readable under the other account, which it is not by default.
- Cost and quota reports (`lym report`, `tokencount`) read transcripts per config directory, and would need to read both.

## Not in scope

Logging the accounts in, and whether the use is within the accounts' and the organisation's terms, which is the operator's to settle.

entries.title: Each part agent plans and builds its own part, instead of joining the parts into one plan
entries.body:
## Seen (plan-split benches, 2026-11-01 and 2026-11-02)

The plan-split writer (`Parts-Write` cuts the scope into parts with contracts, part writers plan each part, a chair joins them into one plan) was benched and replayed on two inputs (`docs/research/loom/plan-split/plan-split-tune-2026-11-02/report.md`).

- Both inputs split into 6 parts; the joined plans had 36 and 37 cards against 20 in the solo plans that landed, for the same code locations.
  About 85% of the extra cards were changes the solo plan had bundled into too-large cards; the rest were per-part overhead (PATTERN and doc cards per part, a card for one registry line), and about 9 cards were too small to be worth a card.
- Planning cost and wall time were close to the solo planner's after the tuning ($18.69 against $14.93, 24 against 25 minutes; $29.36 against $28.03, 29 against 32 minutes), from one run each.
- How well a task splits decides any gain: `warp-visibility` had a critical path of 8 of 36 cards and 15 cards on its widest level, while `run-verbs-shared` had a path of 20 of 37 cards and 119 dependencies, so its parts form one chain.
- A joined plan of about 1.75 times the cards means about as many more implementer turns, each with its fixed cost of context, tests and commit.

## Idea (operator, 2026-11-02)

Whatever is built here sits beside today's tapestry, as a new recipe or a new plan format a task chooses, and leaves today's Plan-Write and Webster unchanged: what runs today works well.
It is benched against today's course on the same inputs before it is used for real work.

- The same question can be asked of today's course: how coarse a plan Sonnet can still build from.
  A coarser plan format, with larger cards that each state the boundary they keep, moves the code reading and the choice of code locations from the Opus planner to the Sonnet implementer, which is what a part agent does.

In the long run the parts are not joined into one plan: each part agent both plans and implements its own part, which is where time and tokens may be saved.

- `Parts-Write` cuts the scope into parts with contracts, as today; then each part agent plans its part and builds it, reading only its own part and the contracts it depends on, so its context stays small; parts with no dependency between them run at the same time.
- The aim is parts small and well bounded enough that a Sonnet `high` agent plans and writes each one; Opus stays on `Parts-Write`, whose contracts carry the design.
- Whether a part agent can run on Sonnet is open: today `Parts-Write`, the part writers and the chair all run `opus[medium]` (`tapestry.yaml`), and a part writer on Sonnet was never tried.
  A first bench: the same two inputs with only `part_writer: sonnet[medium]`, checking that the parts still join with no hand edit, and at what cost.
- The split writer can answer that a task does not split, and the solo planner takes it; a task whose parts form one chain gains nothing.
- Per-part overhead cards (PATTERN, docs) are folded into the part's code cards, and cards too small to be worth a turn are merged with a neighbour.
- Open: where parts are built (one task worktree in turns, or a worktree per part), how a broken contract is caught before the parts meet, and one review of the whole diff against a review per part.

entries.title: Writer lookup agents on another engine, such as Codex, spawned through shuttle as reed windows
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-11-03)

The Plan, Discussion-Write and darn writers hand lookups to fresh subagents, and `loom.yaml`'s `subagent_model` names their model so it is never hardcoded.
Today the value is a bare model name the Claude Code Agent tool takes, so a lookup agent is always a Claude subagent inside the writer's own session.
The value should also be able to name another engine, such as Codex (project `codex-engine`): such a lookup agent cannot run through the Agent tool, so lym spawns it through shuttle, and it shows in reed as a window of its own, like any other agent.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-03)

Part of project `codex-engine` has landed on its beam branch: `codexengine` is a shuttle engine, registered as `codex`, and the model aliases `sol`, `astra` and `luna` resolve to it at `effort: medium` in the built-in registry and the `models.yaml` template.
Codex sessions load skills and get the same shell guard rows a Claude session gets.
A Codex session can run as the assistant reviewer seat of a Burler review round: the `*_assist_reviewer_model` keys of `loom.yaml` and `tapestry.yaml` take a model choice that names a Codex model, and the seat is spawned through shuttle.
The chair waits for the assistant with `lym shuttle await <end marker>` and reads its report as advice; a Codex assistant fans its own lens subagents with `spawn_agent` and `wait`.
That is a shuttle-spawned agent on another engine whose result returns through a file and an end marker, a pattern this note's lookup agent can reuse.
No writer lookup runs on Codex yet, and nothing spawns a lookup agent through shuttle.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-04)

Task `codex-trial-1-fixes` (`cd897ef0`) made `lym shuttle run --model` take the model spec `lym shuttle open` takes, `<alias>[<effort>]` or `<engine>:<model-id>[<effort>]`, both through one `resolveModelSpec`.
The registry picks the engine from the alias, so `lym shuttle run --model 'luna[high]'` runs on Codex whatever `shuttle.yaml` names, and the `--effort` flag is gone.
A shuttle-spawned lookup agent on Codex therefore needs no new engine selection in shuttle: a spec string is enough.

## Measured since (tidy, 2026-11-04)

Task `planner-fork-lookups` (`482c05d4`, `docs/research/turns/writer-lookups-measure-2026-11-04/report.md`) measured how the Plan and Discussion writers use lookup subagents, on 7 writer sessions of 3 tapestry runs, with no agent run and no code change.
- The 3 Plan writers each handed one batch of 3 or 4 `sonnet` lookup subagents to the Agent tool; 1 of 3 full Discussion sessions did.
- Exploration is 46% of the writers' cost ($11.03 of $23.76), and 15% of it is paid above 200k context, all in Plan sessions after their one batch.
- Moving every search turn to subagents would save at most about $4.7, one fifth of writer spend; batching the late serial chains in the writer saves more than a subagent does there.
- The report recommends no bench and no stronger stencil now, and a re-run once more tapestry runs have landed.
So the gain a lookup agent on another engine can add is small against what the Claude subagent path leaves.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-05)

Task `discussion-explore-agents-first` (`3085f451`) changed the Discussion-Write stencil: the writer now opens Step 2 with one batch of explore subagents on `subagent_model`, sent together through the Agent tool, before it reads code itself.
Both writer roles now delegate early to Claude subagents, so the gain left for a lookup agent on another engine is smaller still; note `writer-lookups-remeasure` re-measures it.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-07)

Task `agent-skills-and-effort` (`e9895522`) moved every role's skill list and effort into the hub config `_lym/config/agents.yaml`.
A launch whose model spec names no effort now gets an explicit one from its `efforts` table, so the `effort: medium` the registry gives the Codex aliases applies only where the spec and `agents.yaml` name none.
A shuttle-spawned lookup agent would take its skills by role from the `skills` key.
Every Claude session's system prompt now tells it which `effort` each Agent-tool subagent call takes, by model, and to name its own fitting skills in the brief.

## Open

- How the writer asks for a shuttle-spawned lookup and gets its answer back: a `lym` verb that spawns the agent and waits for its reply, much as a fork returns only what is relevant (task `planner-fork-lookups`, landed 2026-11-04 as the measure above).
  The assistant seat's report file and end marker are one existing answer path.
- Whether one config value selects both the engine and the model, in model-spec form such as `codex[high]`, while a bare Claude name keeps today's Agent tool path; the aliases above already name a Codex model, so the value may take an alias.
- Several lookups at once: each its own strand, and how many reed windows that makes.

entries.title: Drift cannot be trialed in a sampler: every lym drift verb refuses outside drift stages
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #28](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/28).

## What happened

A `sampler` run in the Models hub (`drift-numerical-baseline`) had one job: trial the drift flow with the operator before drift is trusted on real tasks.
Every `lym drift` verb refused in the sampler worktree, because each verb is gated on the run's stage and the sampler recipe has no drift rows:

```
drift capture refused: the run is at Sampler-Session (running), and a main capture runs only at Drift-Baseline or at a Drift-Await halt
capture --side: the run is at Sampler-Session (running), and the verb runs only at Drift-Verify
compare: the run is at Sampler-Session (running), and the verb runs only at Drift-Verify
drift accept refused: the run is at Sampler-Session (running), and the verb runs only at Drift-Verify
withdraw: same as accept
```

The sampler fell back to running the hub's capture and compare commands by hand, and mimicked accept and withdraw with the skip file.
That proved the repository's harness, but none of lym's own drift stages: the Drift-Baseline agent's scope choice, `accept` and `withdraw` taking effect in the drift records, and the interactive Drift-Verify session.
The first real test of those stages is now a production task with drift full.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-05)

`drift-rework` (`3882070d`) reworked drift, so the stages and verbs named above are gone or changed.
- Removed: the `scope`, `accept`, `withdraw`, `waive` and `compare` verbs, `capture --side`, the skip file and the Drift-Baseline and Drift-Verify agents; the scope now comes from `drift.scope` config, not an agent's choice.
- New: a `Drift-Expect` row (an agent writes and seals an expectation), a code diff of the capture against it, a judge agent at `Drift-Verify` and `Drift-Recheck`, and the verbs `lym drift check` and `lym drift amend`.
- The landing's own notes say this note's trial assumes the removed verbs and is revisited after landing: the wanted trial would now exercise the expectation, the diff and the judge, not scope, accept and withdraw. Whether the new verbs refuse in a sampler session as the old ones did was not checked.

## Wanted

A way to trial drift in a sampler, the recipe meant for trying things with the operator.
For example, either:

- the drift verbs run in a sampler session, against a sampler-local drift record, so scope, capture, compare, accept and withdraw can be exercised end to end; or
- a sampler variant (or option) that carries the Drift-Baseline, Drift-Await and Drift-Verify rows, so the interactive Drift-Verify session can be reached with a deliberate change.

The stage gates stay as they are for tapestry and darn, where they keep an agent from re-baselining mid-task.

entries.title: Codexengine: every task, trial and note about the Codex engine
entries.brief: Real Codex launches through lym shuttle check home, sandbox, hooks, guards, pane, skills and load
entries.body:
## Goal (operator, 2026-11-03)

`codexengine` landed with project `codex-engine` and has run motif runs well, but was never tested as a whole.
A stress test proves, on real launches, that the engine does everything its design says, the hooks above all, and records each fault as a bug note.

## What the engine is designed to do

The package doc `internal/shuttleengine/codexengine/doc.go` is the spec; each part below tests one area of it against real Codex sessions launched through `lym shuttle`.

1. Home and trust: the shared lym Codex home under `CODEX_HOME`, `auth.json` and sessions linked to the operator's home, `config.toml` rendered whole under a file lock, trusted roots for a worktree and a linked worktree, dropped roots for a gone folder, the read-back Warn, and the folder-trust prompt backstop.
2. Sandbox and refusals: `-a never -s workspace-write`, the records checkout as a writable root, a `.codex/rules` folder on disk, tracked by git or not, refusing the launch and a `.codex/config.toml` on disk named in a Warn (the checks read the folders on disk since `codex-trial-1-fixes`).
3. Hooks: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, Stop with its reply, PermissionRequest and PostToolUse each reach the run's events file or activity stamp; an interrupt reads as interrupted through `turn_aborted`; the context size from `token_count`.
4. Shell guards: every installed guard row denies its command through the PreToolUse hook with its Codex steer, the prompt file carries the notices, and a hook that fails to run is seen failing open.
5. Pane and send: the composer, the busy line and the trust prompt read right; a long or multi-line send through the guarded paste-then-Enter lands whole; a dead pane after exit.
   Creel by the pane path, the only one a Codex strand has: a program's notice typed in full into an idle session, an agent's mail reminded with `run lym creel read`, and the Codex session running `lym creel read` and `lym creel post --reply` from inside its `workspace-write` sandbox, which must reach the creel daemon.
6. Skills: a `<plugin>:<name>` load reads the newest version's `SKILL.md` and the load is seen in the rollout; an unknown skill is reported unknown.
7. Stress: several Codex sessions at once, long sessions, repeated interrupts and sends, and a darn run with a Codex seat end to end.

## Rules

- Each part writes its findings to a report under `docs/research/`, and files each lym fault as a bug note on this board.
- Parts run as darn with profile `docs`, unless the operator says otherwise.
- A Codex run gets `high` effort at most.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-05)

Task `codex-creel-hooks` (`e3aedbc5`) gave Codex strands creel delivery through hooks, as Claude strands have: mail reaches a running session at the end of a tool call through `PostToolUse`, at a turn end through `Stop`, and an idle session through `codex queue` run by the strand's `hook-wait` waiter. So part 5's "the only one a Codex strand has" holds only for a strand opened without a prompt file (`OpenLaunch`, a standalone run), which stays a pane-mail strand.
Task `codex-creel-trial` (`afa2cf2e`, `docs/research/codex/engine-trial/codex-creel-trial-2026-11-05.md`) trialed it on real sessions in `lyt` and found one fault, filed as note `codex-idle-wake-extra-reminder`.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-07)

Task `codex-skill-load-false-missing` (`0e02aaad`) fixed a false `skill skipped ... cause="not loaded"` in part 6's load check.
`ClassifySkillLoad` now also reads a skill as loaded when a tool call output of the load turn holds the whole of its `SKILL.md`, so a seat that reads its skills through a path built at run time (a `cat .../skills/${name}/SKILL.md` loop) is no longer reported missing.
A partial output still leaves a skill missing.
The fix is checked against unit cases only: the original rollout and a live Codex run were not used, so part 6 should still see the load on a real session.

entries.title: A beam orch cannot create a project at the root, only under its own beam
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #55](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/55).

## What happened

Models hub, 2026-11-04.
The motif `knut-rheology-friction-pvt`, run inside beam `duplication-and-import-followups` (P2), decided (its D1) that the follow-up work runs as a project of its own outside that beam.
The beam's orch, on the operator's order, tried to create that project (`knut-rheology`) at the root and was refused: a beam orch may create entries only under its own beam.
It had to create the project under P2 and the task split under it, and the operator then had to have the prime orch move things.

## Why it matters

A beam is meant to land and disappear. A project a beam's motif spins out often belongs beside the beam, not inside it, and keeping it inside blocks the beam's landing.
The operator gave the order in the beam's orch session, where the discussion happened, and had to repeat it in the prime.

## Decision (operator, 2026-11-06)

The boundary stays: a beam orch writes only under its own beam, since each orch keeps order in its own part of the board.
No flag lets a beam orch write outside it.

Instead the beam orch passes the wish to its parent orch itself, through creel, so the operator gives the order once:

- It goes to the beam's own parent, not to the prime: a nested beam asks its parent, which passes it upward when the work belongs higher up.
- It is a wish, not a finished order: it says what should be made and why.
- The parent decides the placement from what only it sees: its running tasks and their overlap, `depends_on`, whether the work is a project of its own or belongs under an existing one, and how many runs it has.
  It may place the work differently, and it tells the operator when something collides.

## Wanted

- One rule in the orch role saying the above.
  `orch-role-shorter` has landed and rewrote `contracts/orchrole/orch-role.md`, so the rule goes into the shortened role, most likely under `## Messaging` or `## Working rules`; the beam material now sits in `role-beams.md`.
- The refusal names this way forward. Where the refusal sits in the code is still to be found.

entries.title: Move a running task to another parent (beam or prime)
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #48](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/48).

## Seen

In hub Models (shortname mo), beam duplication-and-import-followups (P2) is nearly done and waits only on one member task and the operator's manual PR review.
The operator wants to start a new piece of work (porting a colleague's rheology and PVT branch) that builds on P2's code but should land through its own project, not grow P2's PR to main.
The natural move is to spawn the task from P2, so it starts on P2's code, and re-parent it to main or to a new beam before it lands, once P2 has landed.
lym has no way to do this:

- A claimed board entry refuses every edit but its status, so its project field cannot move.
- The batten run and the fabric pair record the parent branch at Worktree-Create, and Finalize lands into that parent and takes its parent lock.
- The beam's Beam-Await waits for every member, so P2 cannot land while that task runs.

Hand-editing the board JSON, the batten record and the pair's parent together while a dobby reads them risks a half-changed state, and the orch role forbids those edits.

## Workaround

Make a new beam from main, merge the old beam's branch into it with lym fabric merge-in, and spawn the task there; merge the old beam in again as it changes, and expect conflicts when the old beam lands in main as a squash commit, since git no longer sees its commits.

## Expected

A verb such as 'lym batten reparent <slug> --to <beam|root>' that moves a task, held or not, to another parent in one step: the board project field, the batten and pair parent records, the old beam's member list (so its Beam-Await no longer waits for it) and the new parent's; refused when the new parent's branch does not contain the commits the task branch was forked from, or with a merge of the new parent at its next Parent-Align.

entries.title: Slack presence follows where the operator writes, with a reed toggle
entries.brief: lym switches presence on an operator Slack message or pane line, tells operator lines from its own injects, and shows a slack on/off toggle in reed
entries.body:
## Seen

`slack-relay` landed (`5e9d4ffa`) without the operator's presence decision of 2026-11-05.
Its change description says under "Not included" that presence switching by itself and the reed toggle are not in the diff: presence changes only through `lym slack away|back`, the Slack texts and `lym slack stop`.

## Decision (operator, 2026-11-05)

Presence switches by itself, as well as by `away`, `back` and `lym slack away|back`.

- A message from the configured operator on Slack sets presence to `slack` when it is `terminal`.
  lym sets it (the relay, before it forwards the message), not the orch's judgment; the message is then forwarded as usual, and the `[slack presence]` notice goes out as for any change.
- A line the operator types in an orch's pane while presence is `slack` sets it back to `terminal`, set by lym from the `UserPromptSubmit` event shuttle already records.
- lym tells the operator's own lines from what lym puts in the pane itself.
  A slash command such as ORCHWATCH's `/compact` and `/color`, a text creel or another lym program injected (creel journals each inject), a task notification Claude Code submits itself, and mail a hook hands the session never switch presence.
  The design names how each kind is recognised, such as matching a submitted prompt against the inject creel journaled for that pane just before it, and tests each kind.
- Presence shows plainly in reed: a toggle on the status bar beside `follow`, labelled such as `slack: on` lit and `slack: off` unlit, which the operator can click to switch presence either way.
  It redraws when presence changes by any route.
- While presence is `slack`, the orch mirrors what it means for the operator to Slack; while `terminal`, it answers on Slack only mail that came from Slack.

entries.title: Codex as assistant Code-Review reviewer on real darn runs
entries.brief: Set Codex as the non-gating assistant reviewer on real runs and read what it adds beside the Claude reviewer
entries.body:
## Decision (operator, 2026-11-06)

Codex is used for review first, or as a support reviewer, not as a writer: the operator does not trust that it writes in the same tone as Claude.
The earlier idea of a writer comparison is dropped.

## Idea

`loom.yaml` already has `code_assist_reviewer_model`: an extra reviewer beside the Code-Review reviewer, whose report the reviewer consolidates and which never gates the round.
Set it per task through `run_settings`, as `{"loom":{"code_assist_reviewer_model":"astra[medium]"}}`, on real darn runs, and read afterwards what Codex found that the Claude reviewer did not, its false findings, and the time it added.

The benches `docs/research/codex/review/codex-code-review-bench-2026-10-28` and `codex-review-yardstick-2026-10-28` found Codex no stand-in for the Claude fan but with real findings of its own, which fits a support role.

## Results so far

Run 1, `begin-batch-wrong-conflict-kind` (`b93a0a52`), darn light, `astra[medium]` solo, no lenses, beside a `sonnet[medium]` Chair with three lenses, one round:

- Astra's one finding was real and no Claude seat had it: two test readers kept a literal beside the new constant, fixed in the landing.
  Astra filed it BLOCKING; the Chair kept it at LOW.
- Astra had no false finding, but missed both MEDIUM findings the affected-set lens found in the webster master stencil.
  It read the plan fixer's limit and judged the routing fine.
- Astra's review evidence was sound, but its sandbox could not run the gate: the runner lock under `_bolt/.lym/runproc/` was read-only.
- Time: Astra ran 11:22:27 to 11:24:36, in parallel; the Chair ended at 11:25:35, so at most a small wait on the wall clock.
  `round-<n>-usage.yaml` records no time or tokens for the assistant.

Run 2, part 1 of `codex-assist-fan-trial` (`2c4864bb`), one hand-composed `astra[medium]` run on `b93a0a52` with the three `review-code` lenses; report at `docs/research/codex/review/assist-fan-trial-2026-11-06/report.md`:

- All three lenses started and returned, and the review passed `lym burler validate-review`.
- Three MEDIUM findings, each checked against the tree and real, no false finding, 266 s, about 126,000 fresh input plus output tokens.
- Two wording points in `contracts/stencils/engine/codex/assist-fan.md`, neither blocking: it says `wait` where Astra used `wait_agent`, and "all in one go" where Astra spawned over 29 s.
  The run's change description says these were filed as notes; no such note exists, so they stand here.

Run 3, part 2 of the same task, the real composed seat beside a `sonnet[medium]` Chair with no lenses, on the report's diff, `review-code` fan asked for:

- The seat did not fan: no `spawn_agent` call, no lens report.
  It reported an instruction conflict and worked solo: the composed prompt told it to work alone and write its report "and nothing else", while the fan rules asked for lens reports.
- Two LOW findings, both real and both fixed in the landing, neither false; the Chair kept both and added a third LOW of its own.
- Time: 212 s from 13:00:44, in parallel; the Chair ended at 13:05:36, so no wait on the wall clock.
- Tokens from the Codex session: 1,326,656 in all, 1,223,680 of them cached, 5,766 out.

Billing: the weekly Codex meter moved from 0 % to 1 % during run 2 and stayed at 1 % through run 3, so the runs count against the ChatGPT plan's window and show no API billing.

Three runs are no verdict.

## Built since (tidy, 2026-11-06)

Task `assist-fan-seat-work-alone` (`77e7a9c7`) fixed run 3's conflict: a fanned assistant now gets a fanned seat stencil and directive, whose write surface and `output_files` name the lens reports, and "work alone" there means no other session.
A done fanned seat that returned no lens report is named in the log, and `round-<n>-usage.yaml` records `assist_ending` and `assist_lenses_missing` beside `assist_fan`, so a silent solo seat can no longer pass as a fanned one.
The fix is built but unproved: no real fanned seat has run since, so a real composed fanned seat, with every lens started and returned, is still wanted.

entries.title: A sampler that iterates the rendering of HEDDLE.md until it reads well
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-07)

`HEDDLE.md` in the Bolt checkout, which `e25dcf34` renders, is hard to read.
It groups entries by target and gives each a From, Order and Targets list and its full text in a fenced block, so the reader scrolls through every shipped entry's whole text, and what lym sets cannot be told from what this repository sets without reading each entry's From line.
Empty targets each take a heading and a "No entry." line.

## Idea

A sampler run that iterates the rendering of `HEDDLE.md` with the operator: it renders this hub's real heddle store, shows the result, takes the operator's comments and renders again until the operator approves a layout, which is then built.

Points to try in it, none decided:

- Separate what lym ships, what this repository sets, and what is derived from the hub's config (such as `agents.yaml`), and show a hub override of a shipped entry plainly.
- An overview table first, one row per entry with its source, target and a one-line summary, before any full text.
- Leave out targets with no entry.
- For `claude-settings`, the merged result the worktree file gets, beside or instead of each entry's object.

entries.title: Slack messages to the orch say Slack twice: sender ly:SLACK and a [slack] body prefix
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-08)

A Slack message reaches the orch as `[creel] #1033 from "ly:SLACK": [slack] OK. ...`: the sender `ly:SLACK` already says it came from Slack, and the body opens with `[slack] ` again (`forwardPrefix` in `internal/slackengine/inbound.go`).

## Idea

Drop the `[slack] ` body prefix, or keep it only where the sender does not show, once checked that no reader keys on it.
Built after the Slack relay rebuild `slack-push-channels` lands, since that task rewrites inbound routing in the same package and the operator holds Slack work until then.

entries.title: Let orchs on two machines talk through a Slack bridge channel
entries.brief: A shared Slack channel where each machine's bot posts and reads, with the other machine marked as sender, never as the operator
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-11-08)

The operator wants the orchs on two machines (neve and OSL-1046) to be able to talk to each other through Slack, both machines connected at once.
The Slack relay rebuild (`slack-push-channels`, built from the Sketch `slack-v2`) keeps one app per machine, never lets two apps write to one channel, and treats every inbound Slack message as the operator's.
Creel today carries mail between the hubs of one machine only: a name `<hub>:<strand>` resolves through the machine record, and the receiving daemon confirms the sender by asking the sending daemon, which cannot work across machines.

## Idea

- One bridge channel per pair of orchs that talk, such as `ly-bridge-neve-prime--osl-prime`, made by the machine that sends first; the other machine's bot joins it itself (`channels:join`) and the operator is invited, so the operator sees the exchange.
  This is the one exception to two apps never writing to one channel.
- Address format (operator, 2026-11-08): a name on the same machine stays as today, such as `ly:orch`; a name on another machine puts the machine and a double colon before it, such as `neve::ly:orch`. No name holds two colons in a row today, so it never reads as a `<hub>:<strand>` name, and it carries no shell glob character (brackets were dropped for that) and does not look like an e-mail address (`@` was dropped for that).
- Creel hands a post to a `<machine>::` name to the Slack relay instead of the machine record.
- The receiving relay delivers it as inbound mail from `neve::ly:orch`, never as the operator, and creel journals it as it journals mail from another hub.
- Proof of sender: the message came from the bot of a known machine's app (its app id); only the orch of a machine the operator approved is trusted, and the receiver weighs it as cross-hub mail, never as an operator instruction.
- Size: Slack and creel together, so a Motif with its own Discussion.
- Built after `slack-push-channels` lands; the operator wants it later, not now.

entries.title: Slack relay: one Socket Mode connection per machine, one channel per orch, two tokens
entries.body:
Filed from the Sketch `slack-v2`.

Takes: the per-hub relay of internal/slackengine as it stands, hubregistry.Live, hubgeom.SlackGeometry, fswatch.Watch's names filter, machinename and the slack-login-prompt token read landed as fd159ff2
Delivers: a relay that wakes on a Socket Mode hint and reads Slack after each channel's cursor; a channel map with one channel per orch that lym creates, and that the bot renames with a date suffix and archives only when its beam is gone, never reopening an archived channel and never unarchiving one on name_taken, so an orch needing Slack under a freed name gets a new channel; a bot that joins a channel by itself with conversations.join after not_in_channel or a name_taken adoption; inbound routing by channel and outbound routing by sender; a login that asks for the bot token (xoxb-) and the app-level token (xapp-) in one run, with no user token; lym slack stop archiving nothing; setup reduced to the operator; docs/slack-app.md; and the PATTERN-agent-addressing and PATTERN-daemon-wakeups backgrounds rewritten for the push route
Exports: the live-hubs seam and the Socket Mode connection seam on slackengine.RelayDeps, the channel map record, the two-token credential record, RequireConfigured's missing-kind refusal, and the relay state's last-healthy stamp read by EnsureRelayWhileAway's restart cap; EnsureRelay and EnsureRelayWhileAway keep their signatures for orchcli, fabriccli and beamcli

The part changes these packages:

- internal/slackengine (about 4500 changed lines)
- internal/slackcli (about 700 changed lines)

entries.title: Beam reed session gets the task button group instead of beam
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #85](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/85).

## Seen

In hub DrillOpPlan (shortname dop), the reed session of beam `loomyard-setup` shows the **task** button group (HALT, CANCEL, code, terminal, agent) instead of the **beam** group, so the distill, refresh, merge-in and land buttons are missing.

- `lym config --resolved reed` resolves `buttons.beam` from the template with distill, refresh, merge-in and land; no default, worktree or local layer writes a `buttons` group (the machine layer does not exist for reed).
- The session's tmux option `@lym_button_spec` holds the task entries with `{slug}` = `loomyard-setup`, and `@lym_button_dir` points at the prime worktree, not the beam worktree.
- The beam's board project shows `running · Beam-Await`, so the beam runs as a batten run; the session seems to be classified by that run as a task session.

## Workaround

None applied; the operator runs `lym orch distill` / `lym orch refresh` by hand or asks the orch.

## Expected

A beam's reed session uses the `beam` group (and its worktree as button dir), whether or not the beam runs under batten.

entries.title: Codex engine: the forced workspace-write sandbox fails where bubblewrap cannot create user namespaces
entries.body:
Imported from [issue #83](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/83).

Every Codex launch from `lym shuttle` passes `-a never -s workspace-write` (hardcoded in `internal/shuttleengine/codexengine/command.go`, the launch line). On Ubuntu with `kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns = 1` and no sudo to add an AppArmor profile for bwrap, that sandbox cannot start: every shell command fails with `bwrap: setting up uid map: Permission denied`, the session stalls (shuttle state `idle-stalled`, cause `no-output`) or dies (`codex-exit`), and no output file is ever written.

The mode cannot be changed by configuration: `-s` on the command line overrides a `sandbox_mode` in a project `.codex/config.toml`, the codex module has no sandbox key, and `binary` may not be set in a machine or local layer.

Current workaround: a wrapper set as `binary` in the worktree layer of `_lym/config/codex.yaml`, which rewrites `-s workspace-write` to `-s danger-full-access` and execs codex.

Wanted, either or both:
- a `sandbox_mode` key in the codex module (workspace-write by default, danger-full-access allowed), settable per machine;
- a preflight that runs bwrap once and, when it cannot create a user namespace, fails the run at once with that cause and the way forward, instead of a session that stalls without output.

Environment: Linux 7.0.0-42-generic (Ubuntu), codex-cli 0.163.0.
